conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. Thompson. I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You were just brought in from home because of bleeding near your pacemaker site. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, Doctor. I got home yesterday after that pacemaker surgery, and this morning I started feeling pain in my belly. Then I noticed the bandage was wet with blood. It kept oozing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And did you have any coughing or hiccups recently? Sometimes that can strain the area.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve had hiccups all day and a bit of coughing. Could that have caused it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might have. The pressure from coughing or hiccups can reopen small blood vessels. We examined you and found a hematoma — that’s a collection of blood — under the incision from where your old pacemaker generator was removed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be if it keeps growing. But we’re going to take care of it. You’ll need a minor procedure to drain the blood and stop the bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another procedure? I just had surgery yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. This one is much smaller. We’ll do it under local anesthesia. We’ll open the site slightly, remove the clot, and cauterize the bleeding spot. It should help you heal faster.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, as long as it stops the bleeding. My belly feels tight and sore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The procedure went well. We removed about 30 mL of clotted blood and cauterized a small bleeding vessel. The site is now clean and has a new pressure dressing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Is the pacemaker still working? The new one in my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, absolutely. The Micra pacemaker is inside your heart and wasn’t touched. The surgery today was only on the old abdominal generator site, which is now gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried something went wrong with the new device.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, the device is fine. A chest X-ray confirmed the Micra is in the right place. Your heart rhythm looks stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my other medicines? I take a lot for my diabetes, heart, and transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed all your meds. You’re on insulin, tacrolimus for your kidney transplant, heart meds like carvedilol and furosemide — all are continuing as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the aspirin? I was told to stop it before surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. We’re restarting aspirin today. Since the bleeding is controlled, it’s safe to resume it to protect your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. What about antibiotics? I’ve had infections before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. You’re on cephalexin — that’s Keflex — three times a day for one week to prevent infection at the surgical site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve taken that before. I’m allergic to Bactrim, just so you know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. We have your allergies: Bactrim, Reglan, and sevoflurane. You’re safe with Keflex.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. The pain is less, and no more bleeding. I’m hungry — can I eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can start with light food. Given your gastroparesis, we’ll start with something easy to digest, like toast and applesauce.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. My stomach has been slow for years, so I’m used to small meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor your blood sugar closely. Your levels have been in the 190s — a bit high, but expected after surgery. Your insulin doses are continuing as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I check it at home every day. I’ll keep doing that when I go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And keep weighing yourself daily. Call your doctor if you gain more than 3 pounds in two days — that could mean fluid buildup from heart failure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from last time. My heart isn’t pumping as well as it should.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right. Your ejection fraction is around 40%, so we need to stay on top of fluid balance. But today, you look euvolemic — that means no fluid overload.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning if all goes well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep the pressure dressing on for one full week. No heavy lifting or strenuous activity for seven days. And finish all the Keflex — even if you feel fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See the device clinic in one week. They’ll check the Micra and remove the dressing. Also keep seeing your cardiologist, nephrologist, and transplant team regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Final check: no fever, vitals stable, incision dry. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’ll follow all the instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing — take Tylenol for pain if needed. Avoid ibuprofen or other NSAIDs; they can affect your kidney and transplant meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll stick to Tylenol. And call if the site starts bleeding again or gets red.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Also call if you have shortness of breath, chest pain, or dizziness. Otherwise, rest and take it easy. You’ve been through a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Get home safely, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.
